units.title: Building the Agentic Workflow
units.description: Assemble your individual building blocks (model, tools, memory, retrieval) into a functioning execution loop. Examine typical structural design patterns and integrate mandatory human-in-the-loop validation barriers.

lectures.title: Creating the Agent Loop
lectures.description: Implement a custom Python runtime cycle that manages execution states, dispatch controls, and loop terminal indicators.

sessions.title: Receiving a Goal
sessions.description: Capture user goal variables, load the initial system prompt, and initialize the fresh state dictionary payload.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the first session of Unit 4. In this lecture, we are moving from static components to active systems. Today, we focus on the genesis of any agentic run: how an agent receives a goal and constructs its initial state. The key objective here is to design a robust, deterministic entry point that establishes a pristine runtime environment. Because agentic loops are stateful and iterative, any failure in validating, typing, or structuring the input state will cascade through every downstream LLM call and tool invocation. We will visually map how a user's intent is transformed from a raw string into a structured, immutable starting payload.

On the whiteboard, we begin by drawing a clean architectural boundary. On the left side, we write 'The External World'—which passes in raw configurations like user goals, budget limits, or session identifiers. On the right side, we write 'The Internal Agent Loop'. Connecting the two is our main entry point function. The teacher should draw an explicit box labeled 'State Initializer' to emphasize that we do not pass raw strings directly into our loop. Instead, we wrap them in a structured state dictionary. This dictionary acts as the single source of truth that will travel through our cycle. We explain that this state must hold the system prompt, the user's explicit objective, an empty message history list, and metadata like step counters to prevent infinite loops.

Next, the teacher will illustrate a common misconception: treating the agent's memory as a simple string-based append model. If we just append text, we lose crucial structural context like API call metadata and systemic system-level directives. By demonstrating the construction of a nested dictionary, we show how to dynamically inject the user's runtime parameters into a pre-defined system prompt template. We will mock up a safe formatting sequence on the board, demonstrating why we must validate that user inputs contain no prompt-injection attempts and ensuring that required dictionary keys are explicitly typed and present before the first API request is dispatched.

To cement this concept, we introduce a practice exercise. The teacher will ask the class to draft the signature of our agent's main entry point function. The goal of this task is to force the students to think about safety boundaries. They will define explicit type hints using Python dictionaries or Pydantic models and write the code that formats the goal into the payload. The teacher will walk through the room, pointing out a classic trap: initializing list variables, like message history, as default argument parameters in Python function definitions. This trap causes state to leak across different agent runs. We will visually correct this on the whiteboard by explicitly initializing the message history as `None` and instantiating a fresh list within the local scope of the function.

tasks: Design a main entry point function accepting runtime goal arguments.
Format input dictionaries safely before launching the iterative loop.

sessions.title: Selecting the Next Action
sessions.description: Invoke the model and parse returned tool arguments or terminal textual summaries to plan the agent's next step.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by visualising the 'Decision Point' of our agentic loop. Draw a large diamond on the center of the physical or digital whiteboard labeled 'Parser/Router'. Explain to the educators that this is where the raw, non-deterministic output of our LLM meets the hard, deterministic logic of our Python execution layer. The main idea here is to show that we cannot simply pass the model's text directly to Python's dynamic evaluators. We must build a safe gateway. Walk through the scenario where the LLM returns its decision: it either wants to call a registered tool with specific JSON parameters, or it wants to present a terminal answer. The primary learning objective is to show how branching logic in code is derived directly from parsing this structural intent, laying the foundation for automated tool dispatching.

Draw two primary paths exiting the central diamond: Path A (Tool Execution) and Path B (Terminal Answer). Explain the mechanics of extracting structured data out of conversational text. A common pitfall for beginners is assuming the LLM will always return pure, flawless JSON matching our schema. On the whiteboard, sketch out a messy LLM response that includes conversational preambles like 'Sure, let me look that up for you!' followed by a code block, and finally a post-explanation. Show how a basic 'json.loads()' command fails immediately in this real-world scenario. To prevent this, demonstrate how to write a resilient parsing utility in Python that uses regular expressions or string manipulation to isolate the innermost curly braces, strip markdown markers, and validate the dictionary structure before routing.

Now, translate this visual routing map into actual Python conditional structures on the right side of the whiteboard. Show the students how to check for specific key markers such as 'tool_name' or 'final_answer' in the parsed output. Explain how the branching logic acts as a safe railway switch: if the parser identifies a valid tool call, it routes to our execution registry; if it identifies a final answer, it sets a termination flag; if it fails to parse altogether, it returns an error message back into the model's prompt history to ask for a correction. This error-handling loop is a crucial paradigm shift for students, teaching them that parsing failures are not crashes, but rather feedback signals that the agent itself can learn to correct in the next loop iteration.

Conclude the session with an interactive debug exercise. Present a raw, malformed API response payload to the class containing nested single quotes and trailing commas—two classic causes of JSON decoding errors. Have the class trace how their parser handles this input. The goal of this exercise is to reveal the exact moments where code logic must intervene with fallbacks or auto-formatting helpers, ensuring that the 'Selecting the Next Action' phase remains robust under the chaotic nature of model generations.

tasks: Implement conditional branching logic in Python that directs execution based on model-suggested actions.
Address potential parsing failures if the model produces conversational preambles instead of correct JSON.

sessions.title: Calling a Tool
sessions.description: Execute the matching Python function safely using model-generated parameters retrieved during parsing phases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by visually mapping out the bridge between the structured LLM output (the parser's output) and the actual Python runtime environment. On the whiteboard, draw a clear boundary: on the left, we have untrusted JSON payloads generated by an external model; on the right, we have local, secure python execution namespaces. The core pedagogical objective of this session is showing how to safely map string-based tool names directly to real executable references without resorting to dangerous functions like eval() or exec(). Instructors should start by illustrating a simple dictionary lookup system where function names are explicit keys mapping directly to function objects, highlighting how this registry pattern establishes a secure sandbox by design.

Next, introduce the concept of decorators as an elegant, scalable way to auto-populate this registry. Draw a conceptual trace of how a decorator wraps a Python function, extracts its metadata, and registers it to a central map upon module initialization. Explain the dynamic lookup mechanism where the runner parses the 'name' field from the LLM response, matches it against this secure registry, and extracts the 'arguments' payload. Emphasize why validating the existence of the tool in the map before proceeding is the first line of defense against model hallucination or injection attacks, preventing the runtime from failing with confusing or untraceable errors.

Now, dive into the critical step of execution safety and traceability: logging parameters before execution. On the whiteboard, draft a timeline of execution. Mark the precise moment *just before* the python function is invoked. This is where we write a pre-execution log payload. Explain to students that if a tool execution causes a fatal exception, crashes the server, or hangs indefinitely, a post-execution log is useless because it is never reached. Illustrate a structured log schema containing a timestamp, unique session ID, target tool name, and raw arguments. This establishes a clean, auditable trail that allows engineers to reconstruct the agent's exact environment state prior to failure.

Conclude with a practical walkthrough of the invocation loop itself, preparing students for the hands-on exercise. Walk through unpacking the dictionary arguments dynamically using Python's double-asterisk (**kwargs) expansion. Address the common pitfall where the model passes arguments as strings when the local Python function expects integers or nested objects; explain how schema validation or standard type conversion checks must be integrated into this wrapper step. The practice exercise will guide students to implement a robust tool-mapping class containing a decorator registration system, complete with structured pre-execution logs and safe parameter unpacking.

tasks: Write a dynamic function mapper matching target schemas using execution decorators or string lookups.
Log execution arguments before they are executed to secure traceability.

sessions.title: Observing and Using the Result
sessions.description: Append serialized tool outputs back to the context sequence to update the model on current state changes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing the crucial turning point of the Decide-Act-Observe loop: the feedback loop. At this stage, our custom Python runtime has successfully captured the agent's decision to call a tool, executed that tool's underlying code, and received a raw return value. On the left side of the whiteboard, sketch a clear physical boundary. On one side is the 'Execution Sandbox' (where API calls resolve and database queries run) and on the other is the 'Agent Context' (the rolling chat history that the LLM reads). Explain to the learners that the transition of data from the sandbox back to the context is what turns a simple linear script into an adaptive agentic loop. Without this, the model has no way of knowing if its action succeeded, failed, or produced unexpected results.

Next, translate this theoretical feedback loop into concrete structured data. On the center of the whiteboard, draw the schema mapping for a tool response message. Point out that modern LLM APIs (like OpenAI or Anthropic) are extremely strict about how tool outputs are fed back into the context. We cannot just append a random string. We must draw out the matching keys: the specific message role (typically 'tool' or 'user' with a metadata wrapper), the 'tool_call_id' that pairs this observation directly with the model's previous command, and the serialized string payload of the result. Emphasize that failing to match the precise identifier of the original tool call is a massive point of failure for beginners, leading to API validation errors that crash the agent loop before it can even formulate its next thought.

Now, contrast two parallel scenarios on the board to illustrate how an agent dynamically shifts its planning based on these observations. In Scenario A, show a successful weather API call returning a JSON payload of '22 degrees and sunny'. Trace how this structured text is appended to the message array, fed back into the LLM, and triggers a 'final_answer' response. In Scenario B, simulate an API error—for example, a 403 Authentication Error or a Rate Limit exception. Explain why raising a standard Python exception here is often a design mistake. If the code crashes, the agent dies. Instead, we must catch the exception, serialize the error message into a human-readable format, and feed that *back* into the tool message context as an observation. 

Conclude the whiteboard session with an interactive tracing challenge. Walk through how the LLM reacts when it reads the rate limit error in its own context sequence. Show that instead of looping infinitely or crashing, a well-prompted model will parse the error observation, realize its primary path is blocked, and pivot to a backup strategy—such as utilizing an alternative search tool or returning a polite message to the user explaining the service outage. This highlights the ultimate value of flow engineering: designing an agent loop that leverages errors as contextual data to drive robust, self-correcting behavior.

tasks: Format a tool result into the structured sequence log schema.
Trace how the next planning decision changes dynamically once an API error is fed into the prompt.

sessions.title: Recognizing When to Stop
sessions.description: Detect the terminal state where the model declares goal completion and presents the final answer to the user.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this final segment of the Agent Loop session, we transition our focus from active execution to safe termination. The core pedagogical objective here is helping students realize that an infinite loop is the default state of any agentic system unless explicit exit criteria are designed, implemented, and strictly monitored. We begin our whiteboard session by drawing a stark contrast between a typical deterministic function that naturally terminates when its lines of code finish, and an agent loop that runs dynamically based on generated tokens. We will sketch the physical boundaries of our system: the input goal, the ongoing iterative cycle, and the critical exit hatch where the model outputs a definitive final answer back to the user.

To build the structural intuition for termination, we will model the exit condition as a hard schema boundary. On the whiteboard, we will sketch a structured JSON response schema where the model must choose between calling a tool or populating a specific 'final_answer' string field. We will explain to the students why relying on implicit conversational cues (like the LLM saying 'I am done' in plain text) is a recipe for system hangs. Instead, we enforce a strict schema validation layer. If the parsed JSON payload contains a populated 'final_answer' key, the execution engine intercepts this payload, breaks the 'while True' loop immediately, and returns the contents of that key as the final output. We'll walk through the exact conditional logic blocks in Python to show how simple but vital this extraction process is.

Next, we must address the reality of failures in autonomous loops: the infinite execution loop. We will illustrate this scenario on the whiteboard by drawing a cyclical arrow labeled 'The Hallucination Spin' or 'The Error Trap', where an agent repeatedly calls the same failing tool or gets stuck in a planning circle. This is where we introduce the concept of 'Loop Guardrails'—specifically, a hard limit on iteration depth (max_steps) and a running execution timeout. We will visually map how each pass through our main execution cycle increments an internal step counter. If this counter exceeds a predefined limit (for example, 5 or 10 iterations), the runtime halts execution and returns a descriptive error state, preventing runaway cloud costs and system resources exhaustion.

Finally, we will transition into an interactive, concept-first practice exercise. We will challenge the learners to mentally dry-run an agent that has hit a rate limit error on a crucial tool. Without a loop limit, the agent will repeatedly try to call the tool, receive an error, append that error to its history, and try again indefinitely. We will guide the class to design an exception handler that detects this specific repetitive failure signature and forces a graceful fallback termination. This exercise reinforces that loop termination is not just about success, but about engineering predictable failure modes that leave the application state clean and the user well-informed.

tasks: Write condition boundaries that check for specific termination fields (e.g., 'final_answer') to exit the loop.
Handle edge cases where the agent spins continuously without resolving a goal.

lectures.title: Common Agentic Patterns
lectures.description: Explore industry-standard layout designs to build structured and predictable systems beyond single-agent architectures.

sessions.title: Prompt Chaining
sessions.description: Analyze sequential pipelining patterns that pass structured generation values along static paths for low-latency executions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to our first core architectural pattern: Prompt Chaining. In our introductory sessions, we analyzed the raw Decide-Act-Observe loop where the LLM is given ultimate freedom to decide what to do next. However, in production, giving an LLM unconstrained decision-making freedom at every step is a recipe for high latency, unpredictable behavior, and bloated token costs. This is where Prompt Chaining comes in. By converting a complex, open-ended task into a series of smaller, sequential steps where the output of one step is programmatically fed as the input to the next, we create a highly predictable, low-latency, and easily debuggable system. This is a static, deterministic workflow—there are no dynamic decisions about where to route the data; it moves strictly along a predefined pipeline.

Let's sketch this out on the whiteboard to build our intuition. Imagine we are building a sequential code generation assistant. Instead of asking a single prompt to write, optimize, test, and document code all at once, we decompose it. Step 1 is the 'Generator' prompt, which takes a simple natural language feature request and outputs raw code. The output of Step 1 is then programmatically extracted and passed to Step 2, our 'Formatter & Validator' prompt, which sanitizes the raw code and adds structured comments. We then introduce a manual intervention point: a 'Human-Validator' step where the developer approves or edits the structured draft before it proceeds to deployment. Drawing this sequence side-by-side demonstrates that each prompt has a single, highly specialized job, which drastically reduces the cognitive load on the LLM and minimizes hallucination.

To see how this works dynamically under the hood, let's conceptualize a nested helper chain. When designing these systems, a common mistake is simply dumping raw text from one prompt into another. This leads to semantic drift, where extraneous conversational filler from Step 1 ('Sure, here is the code you requested!') pollutes the context of Step 2. To prevent this, teachers should emphasize the use of structured formats like JSON or strict extraction helper functions. We want to extract only the valid code block from Step 1, run programmatic validations first, and only then pass the cleaned, nested dictionary payloads to downstream prompts. This ensures that downstream nodes in our chain always receive pristine, predictable inputs.

Let's pause here for our first interactive practice moment. I want you to draw a conceptual flow diagram of this generator-to-validator sequence. Include the raw user prompt, the intermediate extraction step, the validator LLM, and the human gatekeeper. Pay special attention to the interface boundaries: what exact data format travels across each wire? This exercise is designed to reveal a classic pitfall: forgetting to define how the system handles a failure. What if Step 1 produces non-parsable output? By visualizing these boundaries, you will realize that robust chain engineering requires explicit programmatic safeguards between the links in your chain.

tasks: Design a visual flow diagram of a sequential code generator and human-validator sequence.
Implement a nested helper chain feeding outputs downstream dynamically.

sessions.title: Routing
sessions.description: Build high-speed classification routers that direct incoming user queries to specialized sub-prompts or specific databases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing why monolithic, single-agent prompts fail as they scale. On the physical or digital whiteboard, draw a single, massive node representing an all-in-one generalist prompt, and dramatically cross it out with a red marker. In its place, sketch a clean, modular layout: a central "Router" node acting as a traffic controller, distributing incoming queries to discrete, downstream lanes like "Technical Support" or "Account Billing". Explain that routing is the ultimate design pattern for reducing latency and API costs. Instead of forcing a massive model to process every single niche task with a bloated prompt, we use a fast, focused classifier to direct the query to a highly specialized, lightweight prompt or a specific database. This separation of concerns ensures that each downstream agent only handles what it does best.

Next, map out the anatomy of an industrial-grade router prompt on the whiteboard. Explain that a naive prompt like "Is this billing or tech support?" will fail under real-world pressure. Instruct the teacher to write out three core pillars of a reliable routing prompt on the board: explicit, mutually exclusive category definitions; a fallback "general_triage" category; and a strict output format requirement. Emphasize that models naturally love to explain themselves. Explain why a conversational output like "This looks like a billing issue to me" will instantly crash downstream code parsers. Show how to enforce a rigid JSON schema, returning a single, predictable enum token, so the software wrapper can instantly direct the request without complex regex cleaning.

Transition to the core challenge of routing: handling atypical inputs and boundary friction. On the whiteboard, sketch a Venn diagram where the circles for "Tech Support" and "Account Billing" overlap. Use the highly ambiguous query: "I can't log into my dashboard to pay my invoice." Is this a technical credential issue, or a financial transaction issue? Teach the learners how to design "tie-breaker" rules directly within the prompt constraints, prioritizing security and access issues over billing questions. Explain how to establish a systematic threshold check, instructing the router to default to a safe triage queue or ask a quick clarifying question rather than guessing and sending the user down the wrong, frustrating automation loop.

Conclude with a guided whiteboard exercise to verify router reliability. Walk through setting up an evaluation matrix on the board, plotting three highly atypical test cases against our prompt's criteria. Show the learners how to simulate a mini-evaluation run by tracing the routing path of each query. Demonstrate how adding a short, pre-token "reasoning" step (like Chain-of-Thought) inside the output JSON—where the LLM must write one sentence explaining its category choice before outputting the category key—dramatically stabilizes classification on complex, mixed-intent inputs.

tasks: Write an LLM classifier prompt that routes inputs into either tech-support or account-billing categories.
Verify router reliability thresholds under atypical inputs.

sessions.title: Parallel Tasks
sessions.description: Design concurrent task splitting mechanisms that execute simultaneous LLM calls or tool checks to speed up runtime loops.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back. In this session, we transition from sequential routing patterns to parallel execution. The core premise is simple: when an agentic system needs to gather information from multiple independent tools, or run multiple independent LLM analyses, executing them one after another is a massive waste of user waiting time. We are shifting from sequential constraints to a split-and-merge mindset. On our whiteboard, we will visually dissect how an incoming request gets split into parallel branches, executed concurrently, and then aggregated into a singular context. Since our learner requested a concept-first public lecture style, we will focus heavily on the underlying concurrency mechanics, architectural paradigms, and raw Python async patterns rather than hiding behind high-level framework wrappers.

Let us begin by drawing a fork-and-join diagram on the whiteboard. When a user asks an agent to 'analyze my portfolio holdings and check the latest news on each of them', we have two choices. We can look up Stock A, wait for the response, look up Stock B, wait for the response, and then proceed. Or, we can trigger concurrent API calls to fetch details for Stock A and Stock B simultaneously. This visual split represents the 'fan-out' phase. The 'fan-in' phase occurs when both concurrent streams complete, and we must safely merge their results into a unified prompt context for the final agent decision. The key insight here is that parallel execution is not about making the LLM itself run faster; it is about hiding network latency and tool-execution delay, allowing our flow-engineered agent to remain highly responsive.

Now, let us address a common developer pitfall: mixing synchronous and asynchronous code incorrectly. Many developers attempt to run standard synchronous requests inside a simple loop, thinking it runs in parallel, only to realize their code still blocks sequentially. Alternatively, they implement naive multi-threading, which introduces race conditions and complex debugging states. On the whiteboard, we will sketch the difference between OS-level threading and cooperative multitasking using Python's 'asyncio' event loop. We will write out a clean, conceptual pseudocode block demonstrating how `asyncio.gather()` works under the hood. This visual breakdown helps the teacher demonstrate how the event loop yields control while waiting for external network I/O, allowing other tool checks to progress without blocking the main execution thread.

Next, we pivot to the practical challenge of data aggregation. It is not enough to run tasks in parallel; we must reliably handle their outputs, especially when one or more of those parallel calls fails or returns malformed data. On the board, we will design an 'Aggregation Log' schema. We will show how to capture individual task statuses—success, timeout, or failure—and format them into a single, structured context block. We will run a brief mental simulation: what happens if Stock A's API succeeds but Stock B's API times out? Instead of letting the entire agent loop crash, the teacher will illustrate how to catch exceptions inside the concurrent tasks, return a descriptive error state for the failed branch, and present the surviving data alongside a warning to the aggregating LLM. This teaches resilience and prevents catastrophic failures in multi-tool agent environments.

tasks: Implement basic async calling processes to concurrently execute multiple tool operations.
Handle dynamic aggregation of multiple concurrent outputs back into a single context log.

sessions.title: Evaluator–Optimizer Loops
sessions.description: Implement structured generator-grader pairs to iteratively critique and refine code or copy outputs prior to final delivery.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core limitation of single-shot generation. When we ask a language model to generate complex outputs, like code or formatted marketing copy, we are asking it to compute both the structure and the content simultaneously in a single forward pass. On the whiteboard, draw two parallel pathways: one representing a single-shot prompt that frequently fails on subtle constraints, and another representing the Evaluator-Optimizer feedback loop. Explain that by separating the 'creator' from the 'editor,' we mimic the human creative process, dramatically increasing the quality of the final output. The key concept to landing this intuition is that evaluation is computationally easier than generation; a model can spot a formatting or logical error far more reliably than it can avoid making that error in its first draft.

Next, visually map the anatomy of the Evaluator-Optimizer loop on the whiteboard. Draw a closed loop containing two primary components: the Generator and the Evaluator. The Generator takes the initial user prompt and any previous feedback, producing a draft. The Evaluator parses this draft against strict, objective criteria—such as JSON schemas, length limits, or tone guidelines—and outputs a binary status of 'accept' or 'reject' alongside structured critique. If rejected, the critique feeds back into the Generator. Emphasize to the instructors that they must warn learners about the 'politeness trap': if the evaluator is too polite, it will provide vague feedback that fails to guide the generator. The feedback must be clinical, structured, and contrast-based, showing exactly what failed and why.

Transition the whiteboard session into a conceptual code walkthrough to show how this loop is translated into Python. Sketch out a validation function that acts as the gatekeeper. This function should not rely solely on another LLM call if deterministic checks are possible. Demonstrate how to write a mixed validator: a Python block that programmatically checks physical constraints like character length or JSON keys first, and only routes to an LLM evaluator for subjective criteria like tone or sentiment. This hybrid approach saves API costs and guarantees that hard constraints are never bypassed by LLM hallucinations.

Now, introduce the critical engineering guardrails required to make this loop production-ready. On the board, draw a counter variable tracking the iteration depth. Explain that without a strict maximum iteration limit, the system can enter an infinite loop, racking up massive API bills as the generator and evaluator disagree indefinitely on subjective nuances. Illustrate a break condition where, after three to five attempts, the system either falls back to a human-in-the-loop review queue or returns the best-effort draft with a warning flag. This introduces learners to the practical trade-offs of runtime latency versus output perfection.

Conclude the session with an interactive whiteboarding simulation where the instructors walk through a live trace of a failing run. Sketch a scenario where a user requests a 50-word summary, but the generator consistently outputs 60 words. Show step-by-step how the Python validator catches this, generates a targeted error message, passes it back to the generator, and how the generator adjusts its attention on the next step to achieve compliance. This simulation helps learners visualize state progression and prepares them to build their own self-correcting validation blocks in the upcoming lab.

tasks: Construct a python validator block that checks generated answers for length, tone, and formatting constraints.
Simulate a loop that rejects and refines draft outputs iteratively.

sessions.title: Orchestrator–Worker Systems
sessions.description: Examine how central orchestrators dynamically fragment high-level plans into discrete tasks delegating actions to specialized worker agents.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a critical structural wall that developers hit when their single-agent systems grow too complex. When a single prompt is tasked with planning, writing, translating, formatting, and verifying, the context window becomes cluttered, the attention of the LLM is diluted, and system behavior becomes highly unpredictable. To transition from basic prompt-chaining to enterprise-grade complexity, we introduce the Orchestrator-Worker pattern. On the whiteboard, draw a central supervisor node connected by directional arrows to three distinct, specialized worker nodes: a specialized Writer, a Translator, and a Proofreader. Explain that the core philosophy of this pattern is dynamic task decomposition and delegation: the central orchestrator does not perform the heavy lifting of execution; instead, it analyzes a high-level user objective, breaks it down into structured sub-tasks, delegates those tasks to dedicated workers, and synthesizes their outputs into a final cohesive response.

Deepen the explanation of this architecture by visualizing the flow of state through the system. Draw a 'State Store' box adjacent to the Orchestrator. Explain that unlike standard chains where data flows linearly, the orchestrator acts as a central router and state synthesizer. The orchestrator must parse the user query, generate a plan (often represented as a JSON array of sub-tasks), dispatch these tasks, and wait for callback payloads. As workers complete their jobs, they return structured JSON payloads to the orchestrator rather than directly talking to one another. Emphasize why this separation of concerns is vital: if the Translator fails, the Orchestrator can trigger a retry or fallback mechanism specifically for that worker, without restarting the entire writing process. This isolation prevents cascading failures and makes debugging significantly easier.

Transition into an active whiteboard exercise to compare this supervisor-led orchestration against a single monolithic agent. Draw a T-chart on the board. On the left side, under 'Monolithic Agent', list characteristics like 'Massive prompt instructions', 'High token consumption per run', 'Hard-to-trace bugs', and 'Brittle control'. On the right side, under 'Orchestrator-Worker', list 'Modularity', 'Isolated testing profiles', 'Parallel worker execution', and 'Predictable routing'. Walk through a scenario where a user wants an article written, translated, and proofread. In a single agent setup, a failure in translation requires re-running the entire 4000-token prompt. In the orchestrator-worker setup, we only re-run the lightweight translation worker. This comparison highlights a crucial software engineering intuition: modularity reduces runtime costs and latency while increasing system determinism.

Address a common developer misconception: the temptation to make workers too smart or autonomous. Warn the class that workers should remain tightly scoped, single-purpose functions or micro-agents. If a worker starts spinning up its own complex sub-agents without orchestrator oversight, you create nested execution loops that are incredibly expensive and difficult to debug. To reinforce this, sketch an anti-pattern on the board where a 'Proofreader' worker starts recursively calling other sub-agents behind the orchestrator's back, resulting in an infinite execution loop. Teach the students to maintain strict top-down control where the orchestrator remains the single source of truth for the global state.

Conclude the session with a practical diagramming exercise. Challenge the students to design a visual flow representing a complex marketing pipeline. They must map out how an Orchestrator receives a raw product brief, dispatches tasks concurrently to a 'Market Researcher' worker and a 'Competitor Analyst' worker, synthesizes those insights, passes the synthesized context to a 'Copywriter' worker, and finally routes the copy to a 'Compliance Checker' worker before delivering the output. Guide them through representing the state transitions at each step, ensuring they understand how the orchestrator acts as the glue holding these micro-agents together in a robust, predictable system.

tasks: Diagram a supervisor structure coordinating separate writer, translator, and proofreader agents.
Compare the trade-offs of using supervisor orchestrations vs. a single complex agent.

lectures.title: Human Oversight
lectures.description: Integrate structured human-in-the-loop interfaces to govern agent activities and secure sensitive executions.

sessions.title: Approval Before Sensitive Actions
sessions.description: Build pause thresholds that intercept state mutating operations (e.g. database updates) to request manual confirmation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a critical structural challenge in agentic workflows: how to transition from an uninterrupted execution loop to a secure, human-in-the-loop checkpoint. In a concept-first public lecture style, we will introduce the concept of 'State Mutation Boundaries.' Before an agent modifies any external system of record—be it writing to a database, executing a financial transaction, or sending an outgoing communication—it must transition from an autonomous execution state into a pending-authorization state. The whiteboard will visually map this as a gateway control point, showing the agentic loop pausing, preserving its call stack, and generating an authorization request rather than blindly executing the destructive action.

Next, we will translate this conceptual boundary into architectural code using Python decorators. We will show how a decorator can intercept tool calls by inspecting the target function name or metadata. If the intercepted tool is marked as a sensitive state-mutating operation, the decorator bypasses direct execution, serializes the arguments, and routes control flow to a blocking manual confirmation handler. This approach avoids hardcoding conditional checks inside every single tool definition, keeping our software architecture clean and modular. We must warn learners about the common pitfall of losing agent state during this interception; if the agent's memory or context window is not correctly preserved while waiting for human input, the system may resume in an inconsistent state or suffer from timeout issues.

To cement this pattern, we will design a robust terminal-based approval interface. The instruction will demonstrate how to present the human reviewer with a clear side-by-side comparison of the agent's reasoning, the proposed tool call, and the exact arguments it intends to pass. We will construct a strict conditional loop in the terminal that explicitly requires a validated 'Y' (Yes) to proceed with execution, or 'N' (No) to abort and inject a rejection signal back into the agent's message history. This rejection signal is critical because it teaches the agent *why* its action was blocked, allowing it to replan instead of crashing.

We will wrap up with a practical simulation exercise. Students will observe an agent trying to execute a simulated balance transfer. The program will intercept the request, print the planned transaction details to the terminal, and wait. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners understand the difference between pausing a thread of execution and simply terminating a script. We will conclude by showing how this local terminal validation pattern forms the exact foundation for production-grade webhooks and approval queues.

tasks: Write an intercept decorator in Python that pauses execution if a 'write' tool is selected.
Design a terminal interface prompt requiring a 'Y' or 'N' input from a human controller.

sessions.title: Escalating Uncertain Decisions
sessions.description: Instruct agents to recognize ambiguous inputs and dynamically ask for human guidance instead of guessing or failing.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing a critical architectural intuition: a truly robust agent must know when it does not know. In deterministic systems, unexpected or ambiguous input triggers a hard failure or an uncaught exception. In naive agentic setups, the model often hallucinates a path forward or guesses the user's intent with unfounded confidence, which is far more dangerous. The core goal of this session is to teach the instructor how to visually map out 'escalation thresholds' on the whiteboard, demonstrating how to transform ambiguity from a fatal system error into a structured, conversational feedback loop.

Draw a horizontal spectrum on the whiteboard. On the far left, place 'High Confidence/Clear Intent' (where the agent executes tools directly). On the far right, place 'Low Confidence/Clear Conflict' (where the agent immediately pauses and escalates). The middle of this spectrum is the danger zone: ambiguous inputs where the agent might feel tempted to guess. Explain to the students that instead of writing increasingly complex regex or heuristic checks, we can model 'asking for help' as a first-class tool capability. By equipping the agent's system prompt with clear boundary criteria and a dedicated 'ask_human' callback tool, we empower the model's reasoning engine to voluntarily yield control back to the operator when key parameters are missing or conflicting.

Next, walk the students through the design of the instruction guide that governs this tool-calling behavior. On the whiteboard, outline the three golden rules of escalation: Multi-option Ambiguity (when a user request matches multiple system entities), Missing Core Context (when a task requires a specific parameter that cannot be safely assumed), and Conflicting Source Data (when external tools return contradictory facts). Address a common student pitfall here: learners often write prompts that tell the agent to 'ask the user if you are confused.' Explain why this is too vague; models are notoriously bad at self-assessing their own 'confusion.' Instead, teach them to instruct the agent to look for concrete triggers, such as when two search results provide opposing status flags for the same transactional record.

To solidify this concept, introduce a hands-on verification exercise using a split-screen analogy on the whiteboard. On one side, write down a mock payload containing conflicting search results—for instance, one API endpoint stating a shipment is 'Delivered' and another stating it is 'Returned to Sender'—coupled with a user prompt asking to 'Update the status.' On the other side, sketch out the execution trace. Guide the students to observe how the agent, when restricted by strict system instructions, bypasses its standard write tools and instead generates a structured tool call to 'ask_human' with a formulated question outlining the specific discrepancy. This exercise reveals whether the students' system prompts are robust enough to suppress the agent's natural bias toward action in favor of safe, human-guided resolution.

tasks: Write an instruction guide teaching the agent when to execute an 'ask_human' callback.
Verify that the agent correctly calls the feedback routine when provided with conflicting search data.

sessions.title: Interrupting Agent Execution
sessions.description: Construct safety triggers to manually override and pause runaway execution loops at any stage.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to our session on governing and controlling our AI Agent's execution loop. In this session, we tackle a vital component of robust software engineering: building a manual emergency break. When an agent enters an infinite loop, continuously calling APIs or consuming credits without making logical progress, we cannot simply force-quit the process and lose our valuable context. We must gracefully catch runtime interruptions, pause the execution, dump the active state, and allow for diagnosis. Today's whiteboard session will design an elegant, thread-safe asynchronous safety trigger that safely intercepts executing loops and cleanly serializes the runtime state to a local JSON file.

Let's start by visualizing the execution loop on the whiteboard. Draw a circular flowchart showing the core 'Decide-Act-Observe' cycle. Usually, this runs synchronously or within an async event loop. If an agent goes rogue—perhaps due to a hallucinated exit condition—the naive response is to press Ctrl+C. However, in standard Python environments, a raw KeyboardInterrupt can sever database connections mid-write, leave file handles open, and wipe out the agent's memory history. To counter this, draw an external 'Signal Interceptor' or 'Key Listener Thread' adjacent to our main execution loop. This listener acts as an asynchronous watchdog, monitoring user inputs or system interrupts without blocking the primary agent decision process.

Now, let's address the technical implementation. We will guide the teacher to explain Python's `signal` module and threading primitives. The primary trap students fall into is ignoring the thread-safety of state mutations. If we abruptly kill the agent thread, our memory state is corrupted. Instead, we teach how to set a thread-safe `threading.Event` flag (e.g., `stop_event`) when a specific keystroke or system signal is captured. In our main execution loop, we check this flag at the start of every cycle. If the flag is set, the loop halts gracefully, bypassing the next tool call and entering our serialization routine.

Let's walk through the state serialization whiteboard flow. When the interrupt flag is triggered, the agent must immediately export its internal state. This includes the conversation history, active variables, the last tool called, and the pending goal stack. Explain to students that saving this snapshot to a structured JSON file allows for a 'hot reload' later—meaning we can inspect why the agent got stuck, tweak our system prompt or tool logic, and resume execution from the exact point of failure. Highlight the difference between destructive hard-kills and our structured graceful pause.

To cement this concept, we introduce a brief live practice exercise. Instruct the students to construct a skeleton Python script featuring a mock execution loop that simulates a runaway API calling process. They will write an active signal handler that intercepts `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C). Instead of raising a standard error, the handler must trigger a state-dumping function that writes the simulated agent memory to `interrupted_state.json` and exits cleanly. This hands-on task demonstrates immediately how a simple handler prevents data loss and secures a clean exit path. Watch out for students who try to perform heavy I/O operations directly inside the signal handler thread; emphasize that the handler should only toggle the state flag, leaving the main execution thread to handle the clean writing process.

tasks: Implement basic listener threads or signal catches in Python to detect interruption keypresses.
Cleanly serialize state dumps when exiting an interrupted run.

sessions.title: Recording Actions for Review
sessions.description: Design systematic local logs tracking planning chains, selected tools, arguments, and human inputs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To wrap up our unit on human oversight, we must address the critical issue of transparency. If an agent executes actions, fails silently, or gets manually overridden, we need an immutable, clean trail of what happened. This session is designed to teach learners how to construct systematic, local audit logs. The core idea here is that a raw console output or JSON dump is not readable by non-technical stakeholders or easily auditable during post-incident investigations. We will focus on designing a structured file writer that outputs formatted Markdown reports, serving as a human-readable trajectory of the agent's thoughts, tools, arguments, and human intervention points.

We start by designing the structure of an 'Execution Trajectory.' Draw a vertical timeline on the whiteboard. Explain to learners that each step of the agent's cycle consists of four distinct phases: the Planning/Reasoning phase (what the agent wanted to do), the Action phase (the specific tool and JSON arguments selected), the Oversight phase (whether a human approved, rejected, or modified the action), and the Result phase (the direct tool feedback or error). This structured visualization makes it immediately clear that logging is not just dumping exceptions; it is recording state transitions. Without capturing the human approval input step alongside the tool invocation, we lose the chain of custody.

Next, we address the practical implementation of our Markdown writer. Walk through the design of a Python logger class that listens to our agent's state transitions. We want to show how to dynamically build a markdown file with header hierarchies (e.g., `# Run ID`, `## Step 1: Decision`, `### Tool Arguments`). Explain the common mistake of buffer loss: if the agent crashes mid-run, an unbuffered or open-on-exit file writer will lose the entire execution history. To prevent this, the teacher should demonstrate how to design the logger to write incrementally, flushing to disk or using clean append operations so that even if the agent is killed by a hard system interrupt, the logs up to that exact sub-second are saved.

Finally, we engage the learners with a practical exercise. Introduce a task where they must generate a sample auditable execution log for an agent run that encounters a conflict and receives a human veto. Have them manually trace the variables into their formatted Markdown structure, then check their work against a gold-standard markdown output. This exercise reveals whether learners understand how to map raw, non-deterministic agent states to deterministic, structured documentation, preparing them for the strict monitoring and evaluation frameworks we will introduce in the final unit.

tasks: Create a file writer logging formatted Markdown reports describing execution trajectories.
Generate a sample auditable execution log representing an agent run.
